title: SpaceX catches the Starship to end Flight 15 (spacex.com)
comments: Starship is, essentially, Space Shuttle done right: fully reusable booster without solid boosters (avoids Challenger disaster) and orbiter stacked on top instead of on the side (avoid Columbia disaster).The original designs for the Space Shuttle had the booster (with wings!) return to the launch site, but the cost for two new crewed vehicles was too large, so they scaled it back to the compromised version.Even more revolutionary, compared to Shuttle, Starship is built on an assembly line. They can build a booster ever 4 weeks and a ship every 2 weeks.The future we were promised in the 1970s is about to become real.reply

I agree this is a good approach.But the Shuttle became what it became for reasons that Starship doesn’t have to deal with. Shuttle had multiple masters (NASA and DoD) driving a bastardized design. The non-assembly line of NASA is a feature, not a bug: by spreading work across many congressional districts it mitigates political defunding risk. Im not defending those, but they are important context for those who pretend the differences are a signal of government incompetence.reply

Isn't the fact that spreading work across many congressional districts is necessary rather evidence of government incompetence?That's not a mitigating factor!"Before you walk away thinking the government is incompetent, please remember that the government makes bad decisions on purpose" ??reply

It’s evidence that they are solving different problems. Does the fact that Musk spends hundreds of millions on election cycles mean he’s incompetent, or he’s trying to mitigate a political risk you and I don’t have to deal with?reply
Sure every system has its unique problems but when you cut to the results, one is clearly way more efficient.reply
As said elsewhere, that simplistic take falls apart when you realize there would not be a SpaceX if there wasn’t a NASA.reply

I'm not super convinced that the commercial aerospace industry really needed NASA once super high value satellite services came about in the 90s.The ideal of a good government industry program, is to create a domestic industry, and A: maintain it at a minimum level for whatever goal is in focus (defence, technology familiarity, investment certainty). And B to help it grow to be independent of the government, so the profits and funding can go elsewhere.To me, most of what NASA did after Skylab are a bit questionable. With most of the high profile stuff being of limited value compare to the RF and solid state electronics projects.reply

Can see your point, that spreading the constructions sites across different states was necessary in order to get it built, but in terms of pure engineering, this is probably a negative.Guess the point is that generally speaking, large scale engineering is typically not done at efficient and creative-levels when directed by the government. Governments have too many stakeholders that have needs that have little do with with engineering that need to be satisfied...And of course, there are exceptions -guessing the Gemini and Apollo programs would be a good examples.... oh, and am not trying to call you out, just trying to think through this for myself as well.reply

What makes you think Gemini and Apollo are counterexamples? They were successful, but were also heavily dependent on contractors and occurred when NASA funding was many multiples of today’s budget when measured by percentage of GDP.reply

Well, they seemed like highly effective government programs as they were able to get people to the moon under a very tight deadline (and also knew they were extremely expensive programs. Kind of crazy the amounts relatively to gdp they were spending).And, if they weren't, backs up that the government is not typically a good overseer when it comes engineering programs(although, still seems like when there is a very strong need, governments can be very good partners).reply

title: Lovable apps expose passport details and more than 200K private messages (crissyfield.de)
comments: Hi, I’m the author of this blog post. I submitted it to HN two weeks ago, but it didn’t gain much traction, so I’m glad to see it resubmitted. Happy to answer any questions, though I think the situation is fairly self-explanatory.reply

Technically speaking, is the "leak" or "vulnerability" in Loveable's architecture or in the Supabase database integration?If the real issue is with Supabase then it needs further investigation as several AI tools use Supabase as standard now, not to mention many opensource projects.reply
How many of the 159k analyzed sites leaked private data?Edit: The answer (as neathack tells it) is: 2.5% of the sites. The reply was buried below.reply

From the blog post:  Using datasets from the open web archive Common Crawl,
  we identified and analyzed 159,041 Lovable projects from
  December 2025 to September 2026. Of these, 34,545 used
  Supabase.
  
  24,664 websites sent database records from Supabase as
  soon as they loaded, without requiring a login or any
  other interaction. That alone is not a security issue:
  the data may be intended for public display. But by
  making additional read-only requests, we were able to
  retrieve more database content. We found records
  containing email addresses in 10,560 tables across 7,403
  of the 24,664 websites (30%).

What isn’t mentioned in the analysis is that we ran a System 1 decision model on each dataset to determine whether it contained privacy-sensitive data. Using a confidence threshold of 85%, we found that nearly 4,000 websites leaked such information.Edit: That's 15,9% of all Lovable websites that use Supabase.reply

Don't you think you should have reported this after you established the principle rather than to download more than you needed to do so? Because it looks to me as though you went from 'white hat hacker' to 'quite probably criminal' without a really good reason.reply

Do you think Lovable would be transparent as to the extent of the problem? Or would they use terminology like “a small subset of our users” and “data not including card details” or whatever to minimize the issue.I’d much rather live in a world where independent researchers can figure out the extent of the issue rather than go “uh oh there might be an issue here, guess we’ll never know the extent of it, let’s trust them to fix it”.reply

That's a good question. But it is a very fine line between being a white hat that reports a vulnerability in good faith and someone who actually exploits that vulnerability and turns a vulnerability report into an actual breach. This is - in my opinion, clearly the HN hive mind disagrees - across that line.For instance, if I run into a server and I see 'passport.jpg' in a directory listing I could  download it to see if it really is a passport. But at that point in time I am flirting with becoming a defendant in a data breach rather than that I'm reporting a possible vulnerability. Sure, you could argue that the site owner might close the hole and then they could downplay that it really was a passport photograph. But I care more about the hole being closed than that I care about the contents of the file, which clearly are not meant to be disclosed based on the filename alone.Independent researchers that are under contract with the companies they review sometimes have more leeway in what they are allowed to do. But downloading enough data to be able to run statistical analysis using LLMs is turning this into a reportable breach and that is a great way to get this whole thing to backfire, possibly to the point where the OP turns defendant.reply

One thought might be - did theythe article mentions "we retrieved only parts of the datasets rather than downloading them in full", so a charitable interpretation might be that for each identified source candidate, they spot checked (or had a model spot check) a few individual records to have incontrovertible proof of breach of privacy, and then ran an aggregate count query to gauge the extent of breach. I think that would be fairly in line with "white hat" behavior that's doing the smallest amount of extra work towards a solid proof and clearly not taking the obvious and easy next step of downloading the remainder that would be required for self enrichment. Difficult to argue that there is an intention of malice.A bad actor would be downloading /all/ the data and disclosing it to no one, and selling it while obscuring the source.That said I agree that that certainly might fall afoul of the letter of whatever local laws apply, and certainly prosecutors can also be over-zealous in their interpretations. So personally I would never risk doing something that comes up against that line, from a personal risk POV. But idk if it's fair to argue that this is NOT good faith.reply

I don't argue it is not good faith. I just wonder if OP realized that they might be crossing a line they shouldn't be crossing, ever, while doing security research without being under contract to the party they are investigating.Then at least you are under and NDA and there is no way for the company to spin it that you were a bad guy.The numbers mentioned are pretty serious: "We found records
  containing email addresses in 10,560 tables across 7,403
  of the 24,664 websites (30%)."To me - and please correct me if I'm wrong - that reads like 'we downloaded at least parts of 10560 tables'.reply

Im not sure why you're arguing for an nda. Ive done a lot of security work under contract, the nda consistently means the company will file the report away and never talk about it again.If you actually want change and things to be secured, this post might cause that. I dont understand the energy you are putting into convincing us thats a bad thing.reply

title: How did Woz write the Apple 1 BASIC before building the computer? (retrocomputing.stackexchange.com)
comments: What Woz did was the default way of writing assembly language programs for owners of 8-bit computers (mostly hobbyists).  You didn't have money for a second machine, so you wrote your program on paper, you entered it then tested it in situ.  Mostly you got it right, as doing it on paper was slow and meant you had the opportunity to put lots of thought into it.  8-bit instruction sets were simple enough that you eventually learned the most common instructions by heart.  There was a point where I could mostly translate a Z80 program from assembly to machine code from (my) memory.Maybe that is part of the nostalgia for the 8-bit days: the practice of "slow programming"?  It was relaxing, sort of like those "slow tv" shows.reply

I find it amusing that so many of the comments were surprised about hand-assembling 6502 code. When I came to the Apple ][, assemblers were relatively more accessible, but even at around $200, it was well beyond my financial means so I would write code longhand in spiral bound graph paper notebooks in four columns: Addresses, labels, hex codes (up to three bytes per opcode) and then the assembly code.And that $200 being out of bounds went pretty low: for the first couple years of my programming life, floppy disks were beyond my means, so any code I wrote lived in its official version as hand-written code and would have to be retyped any time I wanted it.reply

That's how I learned to program. I didn't have access to computer as a kid, so I read books, wrote programs on paper and when I got access to a computer I would type in the program and see if it worked. I now have an abundance of computers at home. What a weird timeline all in all.reply

Yes. My first serious program was done this way. At the start of the project (final year of EE degree, 1981) I didn't really understand what a program was, but I learned by studying the technical reference manual for the Intel 8085 CPU. It kind of seemed like magic, I can mold the functionality by storing codes in memory? Wow!I figured out exactly what I wanted to do, wrote it out very carefully on paper, looked up all the hex codes, wrote those out very carefully, adjusted addresses etc. as needed. This took many hours spread over weeks. Then I entered the whole thing on the hex keyboard and display of a primitive development board each time I needed it, perhaps an hour or so each time (I think I only did it twice). It worked first time, because why wouldn't it if you were sufficiently meticulous about your work in a process that was very obviously very intolerant of the tiniest mistake?I must admit my program (gather input information from some transducers, do some calculations, present some results) was likely somewhere between one and two orders of magnitude simpler than a complete Basic interpreter!reply

I think this comment is gold. Thanks for writing this. It feels like such a visceral description of the experience of "programming" back then. I've read a bunch of old books on programming or those that explain low level programming, but they mostly detailed the mechanics of programming, it feels like your comment captured something of the actual experience of it!reply

I got my first computer, a C64, when I was 14 in 1985, and wrote my 6510 assembly in paper as well.You had to carefully calculate the address distance for a branch instruction. The release of DISMON was a revolution: suddenly the computer did all of that for you. It even supported moving pieces of code to a different address to make space for inserting more instructions somewhere!reply
All I had was computer manuals in 1981. I wrote several assembly language programs on paper.reply

Since I learned to write machine code this way, I'll add a little bit of color.You can take the instruction set of a simple microprocessor, and lay out its instruction set in a tabular format. This made it relatively easy to see the correspondence between an instruction in assembly language and its numerical code.Handy "reference cards" were published for looking up the codes, printed on nice thick plastic. You can find these in a google image search for your favorite micro. I got by with a photocopy. Along with that, a programmer would have their own notes and diagrams taped to the walls for quick reference. Machines were simple enough that you really could have all of the vital information available at a glance.Today, the "datasheet" for a sophisticated 32 bit microcontroller is many thousands of pages.Microprocessors had relatively few transistors by today's standards, so the instruction decode logic had to be simple. Logical, if I may say so. This resulted in being able to describe operators and their operands as blocks of bits in an instruction word.I arrived late enough in the game that personal computers already existed, yet I got myself started by hand assembling for the microprocessor circuits that I brought up from scratch.reply

Long before 8-bit computers, I had 15 minutes of access every Saturday to an IBM 1620, so I had a week to write (and erase) code (initially FORTRAN II, later 1620 ASM) before getting anywhere near the computer. When I got to the machine room I had to punch the code on cards using an IBM 026 card punch. For my larger FORTRAN programs, it took most of the 15 minutes to compile them and punch an object deck, which I couldn't run until the next week.reply

My first exposure was Commodore PET computers at the high school (I'm old).  Nobody had home computers then, this stuff was crazy expensive, even a floppy disk (singular!) to save your work on the shared drive (on a dolly - it could be hotplugged) was >$20 in today's money.  But what you could use all you want was the line printer (a CBM 2022) and its consumables.  So at the end of whatever computer room time you could scrounge (lunch, who needs lunch?) you'd print off your 3-4 page epic program to continue coding and debugging with a pencil, on the long school bus ride. This does form "slow" habits.  To this day I detest autocomplete, autoindent, syntax highlighters and the like.  Never did hand assemble though.reply

title: We're Asking an Appeals Court to Require a Warrant for ALPR Searches (eff.org)
comments: I don't think they should be keeping data that's not involved in an active warrant.However, if they do anyway, there should be strong victims' rights protections so that the data is actually used during investigations.There was a string of burglaries in our area a few years ago, and panopticon N-1 (Google Map's auto recording of all phone GPS traces for marketing information) could have found the perpetrators pretty much instantly.They hit rural outbuildings in the middle of the night on camera, so timestamps were precise, but faces were obscured.  A reverse geofence warrant keyed on time of arrival / departure would have narrowed it down to just the crooks with extremely high probability, and other details in the videos would have corroborated the GPS traces.None of the victims were politically connected, so the police couldn't (by policy) run the reverse GPS lookups.  This is the worst of both worlds: Our data is recorded to be used against us later, but if ever it would be useful, we do not have access to it.  The same is true for vehicle black boxes / cameras.  They record a few seconds before airbag deploy, but you usually are not allowed to access them as part of an insurance dispute (even the ones from your own car).reply

Flock and ALPR usage is solved in USA if every state adopts New Hampshire's law:* Illegal to collect every plate for later analysis* Illegal to collect anything except for license plates (no drivers, pedestrians, etc.)* Must delete "non hit" plate images within 3 minutes* Strict forbidden to upload "non hit" camera imagery off the deviceI would add that it should also require a warrant to access the ALPR data, but it's a great start.https://gc.nh.gov/rsa/html/XXI/261/261-75-b.htmreply

This assumes that you don’t get a new administration that decides to throw out all the laws that came before and uses this juicy panopticon camera system in whatever way they want, to do whatever they want.The cameras are an attractive nuisance for people in power, including any and all law enforcement types.  It only takes a few bad apples to spoil that entire ocean.The real threat is the cameras’ very existence, and that is what has to be eliminated.  If a thing doesn’t exist, then it can’t be abused.That’s an important thing to keep in mind, when you are required to keep in mind the lessons of 1930s Germany.  Or the Stasi from East Germany.When you figure out how to guarantee that you can never, ever again have a 1930s Germany situation pop up, and a government that just casually throws out all the old laws, then we can talk about whether those kinds of cameras might make sense again.reply

> assumes that you don’t get a new administration that decides to throw out all the laws that came before and uses this juicy panopticon camera system in whatever way they want, to do whatever they want.What you're suggesting would mean that they wouldn't even have to throw out the laws. They could just install the new cameras themselves.  So there's no difference.It requires a reasonably balanced and trustworthy government no matter what.reply

The biggest argument against limits on storing "non-hit" data that the pro-Flock crowd is going to use is that "we need the historical data to find evidence of the whereabouts of criminal suspects".reply

Counter point police have been able to prosecute crime without being able to defacto track every single person in the US via car and the corrosive effect of having that ability outweighs the gains. Plus on top of all of that they've proven time and time again they can't be trusted to contain themselves or their collegues from rampant abuse to stalk exes, celebrities, etc. just because they can.reply

>>"Counter point police have been able to prosecute crime without being able to defacto track every single person in the US"This is not true, and I dont know why everyone believes that. Real-life policing looks nothing like Law and Order. Moreover, post-George Floyd, police have basically had a work stoppage. Real prosecution requires high agency work by the police and they aren't legally required to do that [1], so they don't, and no amount of voting and police union busting is going to help here. You can't require someone to be "stellar" at their jobs.Having had real egregious crimes happen around me has exposed me to just how much crime you can simply get away with...all the time. The rich get private security and investigators, us plebes get "Sorry no one saw the shooting happen, so we can't do anything now please leave"Flock has basically turned a high-agency job that police stopped doing, into a db lookup, that in some circumstances they can be forced into doing.I agree with EFF, record it all and put it all behind a real warrant and a civilian judge with a high bar for approval.[1]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_v._District_of_ColumbiaP.S: Before you quote Benjamin Franklin at me, no I don't want a 100% hit rate, I just want a decent shot at crimes being solved by average police work and just even the slightest hint of deterrence.reply
Oh, I agree. I just want people to be aware of those potential arguments so they can be prepared.reply

And I personally think that in some cases that would actually be a net positive for society. Like a kid disappears or a body is found murdered or a serious crime occurs. Being able to look at who was coming and going to solve serious crimes is probably a good thing.But for tracking petty crimes and with the abuse of the system with things like officers monitoring their exes, as one example, makes the system far too dangerous for a free society. And because of that if they are going to ever get the public on board with flock then we are going to need to establish certain rights and guarantees.For me that would be things like warrants with the exceptions in only the most extreme cases like a kidnapping or a murder that literally just happened and immediate response was critical. 
Next I would want a reasonable time data was stored then deleted. That is not 2 years that is like maybe a couple weeks or perhaps a little longer. Having the history of when and where everyone goes is a huge privacy risk and should not be stored forever as it is a target. 
Next I would want rules that it is only used for certain investigations and crimes. Yes to violent crimes and sexual crimes and crimes against children and obvious things all of society can easily say yes those things are bad. But for most other crimes it should be constitutionally forbidden. Think of how laws and public beliefs change over time. Imagine this years back when being gay was a crime. Or tracking people who go to an abortion clinic.I could go on for a lot longer about how this type of system is dangerous in so many ways if not governed by very well thought out rules and rights given to the public. It is sad that the operators of these systems don't want to meet in the middle to something that most of the public could get on board with but they obviously know that total surveillance is very valuable data to have on people.reply

The original sin is requiring cars to display an identifying plate.  Imagine asking the framers about a similar ID display on horseback mounted travelers.That's the underlying rights violation-- and it's why solutions that otherwise try to restrict ALPR run into oddities about limiting people's ability to observe what is plainly visible in public.Failing that avenue, we should treat most broad involuntary data collection efforts as a form of stalking/harassment, and treat it accordingly-- including providing a strong civil path for anyone whose data was collected without their knoweldge especially given that law enforcement / prosecutors have a material conflict of interest which will prevent them from enforcing the law.reply
first_paragraph: Today, along with the ACLU, EFF filed an amicus brief in the Sixth Circuit court of appeals in United States v. Sturdivant, a case where police warrantlessly tracked a suspect’s movements using Automated License Plate Reader (ALPR) data. Our brief details the vast, interconnected network of ALPRs that constantly track drivers around the country and argues that this tracking is a “search” under the meaning of the Fourth Amendment. Sturdivant involves a series of robberies in and around Cleveland, Ohio. Using surveillance camera footage, police identified the make, model, and color of the robber’s car, but they did not know its license plate number. After running an open-ended search of two ALPR databases, Flock and ELSAG, officers learned a car belonging to the defendant had been tracked near sites of the robberies, eventually leading to his arrest. title: Why get an expensive Pi when I have an old phone? (thanks.fish)
comments: Nowadays, I just get old laptops with broken screens and take the mainboard out. They are dirt cheap, often even have 16GB of RAM, you can just dump pretty much any linux on them and they are usually way faster than Pis.The boards are of course bigger, which I guess will be a non-starter for many. They'll also require active cooling unless you downclock them considerably. They often also require more power, although many mainboards can be configured down two a few watts of power consumption, depending on what peripherals and speed you need.Yeah, it's more work than just getting a Pi, but given the current prices, it makes sense for me.reply

The goal of raspberry pi's was to have a standard GPIO connected to a moderately powerful and cheap computer for educational purposes. Then it slowly evolved into many use cases because of it's vast community and standardization and availability, not to mention the large number of boards that connect to it. The standardization did erode a little but it still maintains that reputation because of the community and availability and now because its turned into a big brand. Many industrial projects depend on it.If you use the raspberry pi for homeservers or general compute (which I did/do sometimes) then the value proposition is quite poor regardless of pre AI prices unless you have very strict power requirements (in which case it probably fits the above use case already). The comparison with NUCs or mini PCs or laptop boards feels like it's a wrong comparison.The chips used in PIs are repurposed Broadcom SOCs that have inferior bus speeds compared to a general purpose processor from intel or amd, even few generations old. For any general purpose computing these chips will always be slower. its like comparing apples and oranges. I never really understood why people did that.reply

> its like comparing apples and oranges.Yeah, I don't disagree, but I would argue the Raspberry was always an applorange, and that's exactly what made it popular (together with the cheap price in the beginning, which made it basically an impulse buy). It brought people into microcontroller/embedded systems territory without having to actually deal with all of the stuff that made this so daunting. As you said, it is basically a normal Linux PC, just that it runs Arm and has GPIO.
People who are really into electronics/embedded systems will use a proper microcontroller nowadays anyway, these have gotten so powerful and easy to use that there's really no reason for a Pi anymore. And on the other side, people who want a little server, a pi-hole, tailscale  or octoprint or whatever, can just use an old used laptop/miniPC or similar. Since the Pi has gotten so expensive, I see basically no reason to get one anymore.reply

I wanted to understand what actually makes DeepSeek V3 different, so I rebuilt its three main ideas from scratch in pure JAX: Multi-head Latent Attention, mixture-of-experts with bias-based load balancing instead of an auxiliary loss, and multi-token prediction. The model is about 190 lines.It’s a 36.2M-parameter version trained on a MacBook Air M5 (24 GB) with jax-metal, on 207 old detective novels. 12,000 steps took about 2.6 hours.Full write-up with diagrams and results: https://vaibhaav.in/writing/deepseek-v3-jax/The trained checkpoint and exact data are in the v1.0 release, so you can generate text without training.Would love corrections if I got anything wrong :)reply
